title: Cosmic Civilization
text: The possibility of the existence of other cosmic civilizations has always been an important topic in space research. Scientists are interested in finding out whether life exists on other planets beyond Earth and whether another civilization could develop somewhere in the universe. Every year, around 7 stars are created in some areas of the universe, and there are many planets formed around these stars. However, most planets around them cannot support life because their environments are usually either too hot or too cold. Researchers estimate that only about 20% of all planets may meet all necessary criteria and have a chance to have life. Even if a planet has suitable conditions, the possibility of life developing into a complex civilization is still very small. The change of appearance of life from simple organisms to advanced civilizations is extremely rare, which makes it hard to find another cosmic civilization. Therefore, although the universe contains countless planets, discovering another intelligent civilization remains a great challenge.
facts: Researchers ask whether life or other civilizations exist beyond Earth.
Stars form each year and planets form around them.
Most planets near those stars are too hot or too cold to support life.
The lecturer cites an estimate that about 20 percent of planets might meet the conditions for life.
The development of simple life into a complex civilization is rare.
sample: The lecture discusses the chances of finding an intelligent civilization elsewhere in the universe. Stars form every year and planets develop around them, but most of those planets have temperatures unsuitable for life. The speaker cites an estimate that around one in five planets could meet the conditions. Even then, simple life would rarely develop into a complex civilization, making the search difficult.

title: Child Language Acquisition
text: Child language acquisition, three little words. So let's take them on at a time. Child, when to start being a child? For many people, language acquisition starts around about twelve months when kids say that first word, but don't forget the first year. At the first year, our first year of life is very important as well and indeed before you are born, remember there are couple of months before you are born, when you actually able to perceive in the womb, something of the language that's around you. So language acquisition starts earlier than most people think. And it also ends later than most people think. When does child language acquisition stop? Well, in a sense, you know, we are all children, we stay being children all in our lives. There is no obvious endpoint for learning sounds, of course, there is for learning grammar, there is for vocabulary, huh. I mean that goes on for the rest of our lives in million or more words in English. Most of us only have a vocabulary of 50, 60, 70 thousand words, whatever it is until there is always something to learn. So remember that two ends of child language acquisition are wider apart than some people think. That means there is more scope for studying in it than most people think.
facts: People often date language acquisition to the first word at around twelve months.
Language exposure can begin in the womb.
The first year matters even before children can say a word.
Language learning continues into adulthood, including vocabulary growth.
The wide span of language development gives researchers more to study.
sample: The speaker argues that language acquisition covers a longer period than many people expect. Children often say their first word at about twelve months, but they can already perceive aspects of surrounding language before birth, and their first year is important. Learning also continues after childhood, especially as people add to their vocabulary. This longer span gives researchers more to investigate.

title: Bilingual Parents
text:
Many parents communicate and educate their children with two languages, probably because they both know more than one language, or they come from different countries.

Most of these parents think this can benefit their children's language learning.

But actually kids will get confused when their parents use different languages from each other to describe the same object.

If one parent sticks to one language, and the other one sticks to another language, their children will not be confused any more.
facts: Some families use two languages because the parents are multilingual or come from different countries.
The parents generally expect bilingual interaction to support language learning.
The lecture suggests that hearing different labels for the same object can confuse children.
The speaker proposes that each parent consistently use one language.
sample: The lecture considers how bilingual parents use two languages with their children. Parents may both know several languages or come from different countries, and many believe that using both will aid language learning. The speaker suggests that labels for the same object can initially confuse children and proposes a consistent arrangement in which each parent uses one language.

title: A Book of Learning
text: This is the second edition of a book about learning and education. The book is about how to do research. Compared with the first edition, this version includes some updates and improvements to provide more useful information for readers. The second part of the book is specially designed for younger children. It uses simpler explanations and more suitable examples to help children understand important ideas about learning. The new part adds additional content that was not included in the previous edition. These changes make the book more complete and provide a better learning experience for different age groups.
facts: The lecturer describes the second edition of a book about learning, education and research.
The new edition updates the information from the first edition.
The second part is designed for younger children.
Simpler explanations, suitable examples and additional material serve a wider age range.
sample: The lecturer introduces a revised book about learning and how to conduct research. The second edition updates material from the first and adds content. Its second part is aimed at younger children, using simpler explanations and examples at their level. The revisions are intended to make the book more complete and useful for readers of different ages.

title: Library Introduction
text:
There are many functional areas and services in the library.

You’ll see the service desk after entering the library and you can have these services at the service desk.

There are computers with special software on each floor, by which you can gain access to the internet and check emails and library catalogues.

Follow the orange signs and you will find printers. Then, follow the instructions to use them.

Remember to bring student cards. You have to use printers with your card. You can charge your card at the front desk.

If necessary, you can ask the staff at the front desk to help you.
facts: A service desk near the entrance provides support.
Computers on each floor offer special software, internet access, email and the catalogue.
Orange signs lead to printers with instructions.
Students use their cards to print and can add credit at the front desk.
Front desk staff can help when needed.
sample: The speaker explains how to use the library. The service desk is near the entrance, and each floor has computers for the internet, email and the catalogue. Students can follow orange signs to find the printers and use a student card to print. They can add credit to the card or ask for help at the front desk.

title: Edmund Wilson
text: Wilson came then from a different world and he became the focal point of a broad mainstream American culture that thought that modern literature and wanted modern literature to be able to be read and appreciated by ordinary people. They were not modernists in an abstract sense and certainly some of them like TS Eliot and Faulkner were too difficult for some of their writings to be read by ordinary people, but this was a world before the division between the brows or between elite or whatever had established itself as part of our consciousness. Wilson was a major player in the successful effort of his generation to establish at the heart of American life and innovative literature that would equal the great cultures of Europe. And he knew that the great cultures of Europe were there he was not a product of a narrow American Studies kind of training at all. He joined a high artistic standard with an openness to all experience and a belief that literature was as much a part of life for everyone as conversation. He thought that Proust and Joyce and Yeats and Eliot could and should be read by ordinary Americans and helped that to happen. Wilson was a very various man over a period of almost 50 years. He was a dedicated a literary journalist, an investigative reporter, a brilliant memoirist and a dedicated journal keeper.
facts: Edmund Wilson became an important figure in mainstream American culture.
He wanted ordinary readers to have access to modern literature.
He helped establish innovative American writing alongside European literary traditions.
He combined high artistic standards with openness and promoted writers including Proust, Joyce, Yeats and Eliot.
Over nearly fifty years he wrote as a literary journalist, investigative reporter, memoirist and journal keeper.
sample: The lecture describes Edmund Wilson’s role in bringing modern literature to a broad American readership. He helped establish innovative writing at the centre of American life and believed ordinary readers could engage with writers such as Joyce, Proust and Eliot. His high standards were matched by openness to everyday experience. Over nearly fifty years, he worked as a literary journalist, investigative reporter, memoirist and journal keeper.

title: Cloud Formation
text: Absolutely. There's a lot of interest in what forms those clouds. Why are those clouds there, why do they stick around? At the center of every cloud drop is a particle. You can't grow a cloud drop without having a particle there for the water to condense on. The key questions that people have not directly addressed until very recently is what actually forms those clouds. And so the ones that you're looking at over the ocean, it turns out sea salt is a very effective nucleator for forming clouds, so there's a really good chance that those are loaded with sea salt. But as you go inland you start to have pollution come from all different kinds of sources, and so different sources form clouds more effectively than others. And we're trying to unravel which sources are actually contributing to the clouds. The clouds are incredibly important players in climate change in that they reflect the light back to space, and so they're keeping things much, much cooler than they would be if they weren't there. They also play a huge role in regional weather. So we're actually starting to see shifts where having more pollution input into the clouds is affecting weather patterns, and in particular it's actually reducing the amount of precipitation, so we're starting to see drought in areas with super high levels of air pollution.
facts: A cloud droplet forms when water condenses on a particle.
Sea salt readily helps droplets form in clouds over the ocean.
Inland pollution comes from several sources that contribute to cloud formation to different degrees.
Clouds reflect light into space, cool the Earth and influence regional weather.
The lecturer links heavy pollution in clouds to reduced precipitation and drought.
sample: The lecture explains that each cloud droplet grows around a particle on which water condenses. Sea salt is particularly effective over oceans, while inland clouds can form around particles from several pollution sources. Clouds reflect sunlight back to space and help keep the Earth cool. They also affect regional weather, and the speaker links heavy pollution in clouds with lower rainfall and drought.

title: Oracle
text: Technology has greatly changed the way people work and communicate in modern society. One example of this development is Oracle, which has become the largest database company in the world and plays an important role in providing digital solutions for individuals and businesses. Oracle provides many types of services, including emails, voice mails, and database systems. These services allow companies to store, manage, and exchange information more efficiently. For many organizations, database technology has become an essential tool for improving productivity and making business operations smoother. With the support of these technologies, Oracle helps businesspeople travel around while still being able to do business anywhere they need. People no longer have to stay in one specific location to complete their work because digital systems allow them to access important information remotely. In addition, mobile phones have further improved communication. Businesspeople can communicate on the way, respond to messages, and stay connected with colleagues even when they are traveling. Overall, the development of technology has brought greater convenience to people's lives. It has not only changed the way businesses operate but also made communication and work more flexible and efficient.
facts: The speaker uses Oracle to illustrate how digital systems changed work and communication.
Oracle is described as a major database company offering email, voicemail and database services.
Businesses use these services to store, manage and exchange information efficiently.
Remote access lets businesspeople keep working while travelling.
Mobile phones help people respond to messages and stay in touch with colleagues.
sample: The lecture uses Oracle as an example of technology changing business. Its databases and communication services help organisations store, manage and share information more efficiently. Remote access means people can conduct business while travelling, and mobile phones let them respond to messages and stay in contact with colleagues. Together these changes make work more flexible and convenient.

title: Knee Cracking
text: The sound of a cracking knee isn't particularly pleasant. But it gets worse when you listen up close. "It does for most people. But for me, it actually just makes me excited." Omer Inan, an electrical engineer at Georgia Tech. "I actually feel like there's some real information in them that can be exploited for the purposes of helping people with rehab." Inan's experience with cracking knees goes back to his days as an undergrad at Stanford, where he threw discus. "If I had a really hard workout, then the next day, of course, I'd be sore, but I'd also sometimes feel this basically catching or popping or creaking every now and then in my knee." A few years later, he found himself building tiny microphones at a high-end audio company. So when he got to Georgia Tech and heard the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, DARPA, wanted better tech for knee injuries, he thought: why not strap tiny microphones to people's knees, to eavesdrop as their legs bend? "What we think it is, is the cartilage and bone rubbing against each other, the surfaces inside the knee rubbing against each other, during those movements." He and a team of physiologists and engineers built a prototype with stretchy athletic tape and a few tiny mics and skin sensors. And preliminary tests on athletes suggest the squishy sounds the device picks up are more erratic, and more irregular, in an injured knee than in a healthy one. Which Inan says might allow patients and doctors to track healing after surgery. Details appear in the IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. "The primary application we're targeting at first is to give people a decision aid during rehabilitation, following an acute knee injury, to help them understand when they can perform particular activities, and when they can move to different intensities of particular activities." A useful thing to take a crack at.
facts: Georgia Tech engineer Omer Inan proposed listening to knee sounds to help with rehabilitation.
A prototype used athletic tape, small microphones and skin sensors.
The team hypothesised that cartilage and bone surfaces make the sounds as the knee bends.
Preliminary tests found more irregular sounds in injured knees than in healthy knees.
The device could help patients and doctors track recovery and decide when to increase activity.
sample: The lecture describes Omer Inan’s research on knee sounds as a possible aid to rehabilitation. His team used tiny microphones and skin sensors to record movement in the joint, where cartilage and bone surfaces may rub together. Early tests found less regular sounds in injured knees. Such measurements could help patients and doctors track recovery after surgery and decide when a patient can increase activity.

title: Happiness and Social Relations
text:
Happiness comes from frequency and quality of social relation.

The higher the frequency is, the more happiness relations with friends and family and others produce.

It is not sure why social relation is correlated with happiness.

But there's evidence that when people feel more satisfied with their social relations, they will feel happier, in turn, when people feel happier, they will get more satisfied with social relations.

Happy people tend to be social more with friends and have more interaction between family.

Some people wonder if their social activities make them happier or their happy personalities drive them to be social more with their friends and families.
facts: The lecture links the frequency and quality of social relationships to happiness.
Satisfying relationships may make people happier, and happier people may feel more satisfied with those relationships.
Happy people tend to interact more with friends and family.
The direction of causation between sociability and happiness is uncertain.
sample: The lecture links happiness with frequent and satisfying relationships with friends and family. People who are more satisfied with those relationships tend to feel happier, and happier people often interact more with others. The speaker leaves open the question of whether social activities make people happier or people with happier dispositions seek out more social contact.

title: Ageing Population
text:
As the world population grows, the problem of an ageing population has become more serious globally. This is not just a future concern—it is happening right now. About nine percent of people are more than sixty-five years old in the world.

Let's take a closer look at specific examples: Ageing population percentage in the US is now 13% and is expected to be 23% by 2030. About 4% of the UK population is over the age of 75. The situation is more severe in Japan and Italy. And Germany follows, whose percentage of people over sixty-five years old is expected to be twenty-five percent by 2030. These figures reveal a clear trend: industrialized nations are experiencing the most rapid growth in older populations.

The ageing problem is related to industrialization. Industrialized societies tend to have better healthcare, nutrition, and living standards, which allow people to live longer. At the same time, as countries develop economically, birth rates often decline. This combination of people living longer and fewer babies being born naturally leads to an older average age for the population.
facts: The lecture states that about nine percent of the world's population is over sixty-five.
It projects an increase in the US share from 13 to 23 percent by 2030 and a German share of 25 percent.
Japan and Italy are cited as places with more pronounced ageing.
Better healthcare, nutrition and living standards let people live longer.
Lower birth rates and longer lives raise the average age of industrialised populations.
sample: The lecture explains why populations are ageing, especially in industrialised countries. The speaker cites figures for the United States and Germany and projects rising proportions of people over sixty-five by 2030. Better healthcare, nutrition and living standards allow people to live longer, while economic development often brings lower birth rates. Together, longevity and fewer births raise the average age.

title: Robot and Human
text:
Why is it difficult to make a robot like a human being? Why cannot robots finish the work easily like human beings?

For some tasks, it is easy and simple for humans to complete, but it is very difficult to ask a robot to do what we want because humans and robots have different recognition functions.

For example, considering the insights, it is hard for robots to recognize colors because they do not have sensory mechanisms.

Artificial intelligence scientists have to devise a sensor that is implanted to robots to enable them to recognize different colors.

The sensor has a camera on it to capture pixels, and then will translate the pixels into an image, which is not as easy as expected. This process is very complex.

The translation of every pixel to accurate things could be difficult, especially color differentiation which needs complicated sensors to fulfil. So the improvement of the sensor is necessary.

In conclusion, there is no comparison between humans and robots.
facts: The lecture contrasts human recognition with the difficulty of programming the same abilities in robots.
Colour recognition is an example because robots need a designed sensing mechanism.
A camera sensor captures pixels that must be translated into an image.
Accurate colour differentiation requires more sophisticated sensors.
sample: The speaker explains why robots find some tasks difficult even when humans perform them easily. Colour recognition is one example. A robot needs a sensor with a camera to capture pixels and interpret them as an image. Making that interpretation accurate, especially for different colours, is complex, so progress depends on improving the sensors.

title: Survey
text: Let's say if I'm asking which source do you often use to get information. Newspaper? Radio? And the survey shows 62% of the people chose internet. You might be thinking I am going to say, how important the internet is, or how quickly it has changed the world for a few years. But what if I tell you this survey is conducted on the website global and mail.com? Our answer will be different. Because the people who did this survey on a website must be frequent users of internet. This sample is a biased sample. So we have to pay attention to how a survey is conducted.
facts: The lecturer considers a survey about how people obtain information.
The survey reports that 62 percent of respondents chose the internet.
A survey published on a website is likely to reach frequent internet users.
How a sample is recruited affects how its results should be interpreted.
sample: The lecturer used a survey on sources of information to explain sampling bias. Although 62 percent of respondents chose the internet, the survey was run on a website that would naturally attract internet users. The result therefore reflects the people reached by the survey. The lecturer advises checking how a survey was conducted before interpreting its figures.

title: Linguistic Training
text:
I think with our linguistic training we also get all this invisible training to be authorities, to be the people who know. It is part of that process that you come out as a world authority on your chosen subject. But when we move into working with communities, we have to recognise that the communities have to be the authority in their language.

Actually, a woman in the class I'm teaching at Sydney at the moment, a career woman, expressed this very nicely, although she was talking about something else, she was distinguishing expertise from authority. And certainly linguists, because of our training we do, have expertise in certain very narrow areas of language, but we don't have the authority over what to do with that knowledge or what to do with other knowledge that the community produces.

I guess for me the bottom line is languages are lost because of the dominance of one people over another. That's not rocket science, it's not hard to work that out. But then what that means is if in working with language revival we continue to hold the authority, we actually haven't done anything towards undoing how languages are lost in the first place, so in a sense the languages are still lost if the authority is still lost.
facts: Linguistic training can encourage specialists to see themselves as authorities.
A student’s distinction between expertise and authority frames the lecturer’s argument.
Linguists have specialised expertise and communities hold authority over their own languages and knowledge.
Dominance by one group over another contributes to language loss.
Language revival must respect community authority to address that cause.
sample: The lecture distinguishes linguistic expertise from authority. Training gives linguists specialised knowledge, but the speaker argues that communities should control decisions about their own languages and the knowledge they produce. Language loss is linked to one group’s dominance over another. Giving communities authority in language revival therefore addresses a cause of the loss.

title: European Economic Structure
text: After the recession era Europe confronted a change in economy structures in Europe. After industrial revolution around the 19th century, the machinery was widely used in the manufacturing, so the production in factories increased. As a result, circulation of goods became faster, and this led to more accumulation of social wealth. Because of this, the population of middle class expanded and this resulted in the additional accumulation of wealth. This research that conducted by pioneering scientists examined the extent and patterns of structural changes that have occurred in European economies during the recent crisis using some stylized facts on changing output and employment structures at a detailed sectoral level. Focusing mainly on the new EU member states, we compare the performance of various European countries by looking at the differentiated impact of the recent crisis on structural shifts in their economy. We start with stylized facts related to output and employment structures at broader sectorial (NACE-2) level and attempt to find out whether there has been a structural convergence (or divergence) of the New EU Member States (NMS) compared to the more advanced 'old' EU countries (OMS) during the crisis. Finally, we provide also some policy conclusions related to the future role of the NMS in the economy of an integrated Europe, especially in view of post-crisis growth challenges. The financial crisis 2008-2011 adversely affected the manufacturing industry more than services--particularly in terms of employment--and accelerated structural change in favor of the services sector. The latter tendency was more pronounced in the NMS though even here country-specific differences were remarkable. The importance of industry in this group of countries remains strong. There has been no EU-wide uniform pattern of structural change; the formulation of industrial policy at the EU level-- even reaching the 20% target of industry's share in GDP--is challenging and hardly attainable.
facts: Mechanised manufacturing in the Industrial Revolution increased output, speeded up distribution and helped grow the middle class.
The research compares sectoral output and employment shifts in newer and older EU member states during the crisis.
The 2008–2011 crisis affected manufacturing more severely than services, especially in employment.
The shift toward services was stronger in newer member states and varied from country to country.
Different patterns and the continuing importance of industry complicate common EU industrial policy.
sample: The lecture compares shifts in European economies during the 2008 to 2011 crisis. The study examines output and employment in newer and older EU member states. Manufacturing employment was hit harder than services, and the shift towards services was more pronounced in newer members. Industry remained important, and patterns varied across countries, which made a common EU industrial policy and its industry target difficult to achieve.

title: Salary Types
text:
Straight salary sales compensation plans aren't very common, but they do have a place in some organizations. With this type of structure, you'd pay your sales people a straight albeit competitive salary like all of your other employees, and nothing else. No bonuses, no commissions, and few, if any, sales incentives.

This type of compensation plan is most often used when the industry you operate within prohibits direct sales, when sales people work as part of small groups or teams and all contributions are equal, when your sales team is relatively small, or when your sales people are expected to spend much of their time on other responsibilities other than selling.

However, these plans don't tend to offer motivation to sales people, as there are no incentives for them to work harder.

Salary plus commission sales compensation plans are possibly the most common plans used today. They're structured in a way that sales people receive a lower base salary along with commission pay that makes up the majority of the total compensation.

Organizations use salary plus commission sales compensation plans when there are opportunities to support all sales people on this structure and when there are proper metrics in place for tracking sales to ensure that the splits are fair and accurate.

This type of plan is often the better choice as opposed to straight salary because it offers motivation to increase productivity and to achieve goals. It also offers more stability. Sales people will still get some types of pay even if they're in training, when sales are low during certain months, or if market conditions get volatile. However, it can be more complex to administer.

Commission only sales compensation plans are exactly what they sound like you pay your sales people for the sales they bring in and nothing else. There is no guarantee of income.

These types of plans are easier to administer than salary plus commission and provide better value for your money paid as they are based solely on sales achieved. They also tend to attract fewer candidates, but do attract the most top-performing and hardest working sales professionals who know they can make a good income because they know how to sell. On the other hand, though, they can create aggression within your sales team and low income security, which can lead to a high turnover rate, and sales rep burnout from stress.
facts: A straight salary provides fixed pay with little sales incentive and can fit small teams or staff with other duties.
A combination plan offers a lower base salary plus commission, often using metrics to allocate credit.
The combination gives motivation and income stability but takes more administration.
Commission-only pay depends entirely on sales and provides no guaranteed income.
Commission-only plans can attract strong sellers but may increase pressure, turnover and burnout.
sample: The lecture compares three ways of paying sales staff. A fixed salary may suit teams with shared duties, although it gives little incentive to sell more. A base salary with commission combines stability and motivation, and it requires accurate tracking. Commission-only pay is simpler to run and may attract strong sellers, but the lack of guaranteed income can increase stress and turnover.

title: Human Behavior
text: Determinant, human behavior is affected by internal and external factors. At the end of lecture, the speaker mentioned that psychologists are interested in explaining human behavior. Determinant is influenced by two factors, the personal factors which are internal and the environmental factors which are external. The personal factors include people's belief on certain things and their individual thinking about it, while the environmental factors include temperature, air pressure and the others' thinking about them. In conclusion, one's determinants are affected by both himself and the environment.
facts: Psychologists are interested in explaining what determines human behaviour.
Internal personal factors include a person's beliefs and ways of thinking.
External influences include environmental factors such as temperature and air pressure.
Other people's views can also form part of the person's external environment.
The lecture concludes that both personal and environmental factors influence behaviour.
sample: The lecture explains that psychologists study human behaviour by looking at both personal and environmental factors. Internal influences include a person’s beliefs and how they think about a situation. External influences include conditions such as temperature and air pressure, as well as other people’s views. The speaker concludes that behaviour reflects these personal and environmental influences together.

title: Early Robot
text: This is a kind of object that you're probably all familiar with when you had the term robot, but I'm gonna show you the very, very first robots. These were the very first robots. They were characters in a play in the 1920s called Rossum's Universal Robots and they, the play was written by Czech writer called Karel Capek. And basically, these robots, you know, people tend to think of robots as kind of cute cuddly toys or, you know, Hollywood depictions kind of devoid of politics. But the first robots were actually created and imagined in a time of absolute political turmoil. You just had the First World War, you know, it finished had a devastating impact across Europe and so people will kind and people are kind of reflecting on what does it mean to be human, what makes us human, those kinds of question. And this kind of context is what inspired Capek to kind of write this play. And interestingly, these robots being human, they are actually in the play assembled on a production line, a bit like the Ford manufacturing production line. So even though they are human, they are assembled and these robots are designed to labor, and that is their primary purpose in society.
facts: The lecturer traces the first fictional robots to Karel Capek’s 1920s play Rossum's Universal Robots.
The First World War and the political turmoil that followed shaped the play's context.
The era prompted reflection on what it means to be human.
The play's human-like robots were assembled on a production line, compared to Ford's.
The robots were made primarily to work.
sample: The speaker traces the early idea of robots to Karel Capek’s play Rossum’s Universal Robots. It was written in the political turmoil after the First World War, when people were questioning what it meant to be human. The play’s robots appeared human and were assembled on a production line similar to Ford’s. Their chief purpose was labour.

title: Wind Turbine
text: Wind turbine is a device that will convert wind into mechanical movement, which we can use to power water pump or electricity generator. Now the power that the turbine creates is obviously depended on the wind speed, it also depended obviously on the number of sails, the area of the sails and the angle of the sails makes to the wind. So you can imagine if the turbine blades flat onto the wind, the wind's going to just bend it, if there is slight angle when the wind hits it, it's going to turn the blades. We can use that for powering things. Now, we're going to have a go, making some of the very, very simple paper windmills, a sort of things that you can make from the bits and pieces lying around home, and use that to drive very small generator to power electronic devices.
facts: Wind turbines convert wind energy into mechanical movement that can drive a pump or generator.
Output depends on wind speed and the number, area and angle of the blades.
Wind can bend a flat blade, while a slight angle makes it turn.
A simple paper windmill can demonstrate driving a small generator.
sample: The lecture explains how a wind turbine turns the wind into mechanical movement for a pump or generator. Its power depends on wind speed and on how many blades it has, their surface area and their angle. Blades angled slightly into the wind can rotate. The speaker proposes making a simple paper windmill to demonstrate powering a small electrical device.

title: Facial Recognition
text: Last week we talked about how people recognize objects and really how well people recognize objects, given how difficult the problem is, given how objects can be seen in all different sorts of illumination, in different positions, in different angles. And yet we are able to extract that information, we are able to take the visual stuff out there, interpret it in a way that allows us to recognize all the different things that we can see in our environment. Today we're gonna kind of carry on looking at that, but we gonna look at what's really a special class of objects. That's the human face. So we gonna look at how we recognize human faces and how we do it quite as well as we do. We're really expert at recognizing faces. So again we can think about how do we take that visual information and how do we transform it into a form which allows us to put a name to a face, and to do all the other clever things that we can do with faces. So I'm gonna start off again by just pointing out that it's a hard problem. Face recognition is a hard problem, and it's a clever thing we do. If you think about all the different types of faces you can recognize, and all the different types of information you can get from the face, you kind of start to appreciate how well we can do face recognition.
facts: People recognize objects across changes in lighting, position and viewing angle.
The lecture turns from recognizing objects generally to recognizing human faces.
People transform visual information into a representation that can identify a familiar face.
The variety of faces and the information they convey make this a difficult task.
sample: The lecturer moves from general object recognition to recognizing human faces. People can interpret objects in different lighting, positions and angles. With faces they can use visual information to identify someone and extract other details. The speaker emphasizes how difficult this is given the variety of faces, and how skilled people are at doing it.

title: Glass Ceiling
text: The concept of the glass ceiling is a metaphor used to describe inequality in workplaces and society. It represents an invisible barrier that prevents a given demographic from achieving higher positions, even when they have the necessary abilities and qualifications. The glass ceiling often affects minorities and other disadvantaged groups. Although they may have opportunities to develop their careers, they can face difficulties when rising beyond a certain level in an organizational hierarchy. These barriers are not always obvious, but they can limit people's chances of reaching senior positions. One important example is the changing women’s role in professional fields. In areas such as surgery, women have gradually gained more opportunities and are becoming more involved in leadership in surgery. They are not only participating in medical practice but also taking greater responsibility for making decisions. However, the existence of the glass ceiling shows that equal opportunities have not been fully achieved. Removing these invisible barriers requires changes in workplace culture, social attitudes, and systems of promotion so that people can advance based on their abilities rather than their background.
facts: A glass ceiling is a hidden barrier to advancement despite relevant qualifications and abilities.
Minorities and other disadvantaged groups may encounter barriers when seeking senior positions.
Women have gained opportunities and decision-making roles in fields such as surgery.
Workplace culture, social attitudes and promotion systems influence access to leadership.
sample: The lecture explains the glass ceiling as an invisible limit on how far qualified people can advance. It particularly affects minority and disadvantaged groups. Women in surgery have gained leadership and decision-making responsibilities, while barriers to equal opportunity persist. The speaker calls for changes in workplace culture, attitudes and promotion practices so advancement reflects ability.

title: Procedure
text: Procedural fairness enables one party to see the other's evidence, and provides opportunities to question the other party. One party hands in evidence, the evidence is questioned by the opposite party, and then new evidence is handed in again. But procedural fairness actually influences substantive fairness. How dose such a procedure guarantee justice. The case upholds the access to justice as a fundamental right by affirming that citizens cannot be deprived of the judicial review power of high courts and the Supreme Court. It ensures that the decisions of administrative tribunals are subject to scrutiny. It also emphasizes procedural fairness in the functioning of administrative tribunals. It enables one party to see the other's evidence, and provides opportunities to question the other party. When the evidence is questioned by the opposite party, new evidence can be handed in again.
facts: Procedural fairness gives parties access to evidence and the chance to question it.
Parties can provide further evidence after the other side challenges what has been submitted.
Fair procedures influence the fairness of substantive decisions.
Judicial review by higher courts safeguards access to justice and allows scrutiny of administrative tribunals.
sample: The lecture links procedural fairness with just outcomes. Each side can see and challenge the other side’s evidence and can submit more evidence in response. The speaker describes a case that treats access to justice as fundamental and preserves judicial review by the high courts and Supreme Court, allowing decisions of administrative tribunals to be scrutinized.

title: Animal Behavior (B)
text: Why should we bother studying animal behavior? Well, first and foremost, because we are interested in understanding why animals do what they do. There are lots of other reasons for studying animal behavior. Conservation biologists need to know what animals do if they're going to save them. Are those animals social or solitary? How much space do they need and how many mates do they have? Sometimes you can’t predict the outcome of the research. Fernando Nottebohm started out being interested in how birds know what to sing. Yet his research eventually led to a complete overhaul of the entire field of neurobiology, a totally unanticipated yet utterly monumental effect. And this is the course textbook by John Alcock the fact that this is in its ninth edition tells you how fast an afield animal behavior is. There are lots of new developments.
facts: Animal behaviour research investigates why animals act as they do and informs conservation.
Social habits, space requirements and mating behaviour can help conservation biologists protect a species.
Fernando Nottebohm’s work on how birds know what to sing unexpectedly influenced neurobiology.
The ninth edition of John Alcock’s textbook illustrates how quickly the field develops.
sample: The lecture describes practical and scientific reasons for studying animal behaviour. Conservationists need to understand animals’ social habits, space and mating needs. The speaker explains that Fernando Nottebohm’s research on birdsong unexpectedly transformed neurobiology. The many editions of John Alcock’s textbook also illustrate how rapidly research on animal behaviour develops.

title: Housing Affordability
text: The impact on young Australians who are interested in buying a home of their own has been very significant. Australia's housing affordability now shapes the typical housing cycle or housing career as some people call it. Most Australians in the normal course of events are people who move through the housing cycle in a way that matches the stages of life that they're at. So, they move out of the family home in their late eighteens or early 20s as they gain their independence from their families, then they rent save for a home they can afford as either a group, or maybe a couple. And maybe they can upgrade it when they have a family in their middle age, they are more than likely to have paid off their mortgage. And that means they have housing security in their old age. That's no longer the typical housing cycle for Australians, young people generally live at home for much longer than they once did. They generally rent for longer and they're more likely to be saddled with a mortgage not just into their middle age but more often than not into their retirement as well. In fact, in 2006, 65,000 retiree households were still paying off the mortgage. Affordable rent is also an elusive right around Australia. We have very low rental vacancies, we see high turnover as landlords want to maximize their profits in tight market, and we see less long-term or lifelong rental, as we see in other countries and other economies.
facts: Housing affordability has changed the typical path to home ownership in Australia.
Previously young adults often left home, rented and saved, bought a home and repaid the mortgage before old age.
Young people now tend to live with family and rent for longer, and mortgages can continue into retirement.
The speaker cites 65,000 retiree households still paying a mortgage in 2006.
Low rental vacancies and high turnover make secure long-term renting harder to find.
sample: The lecturer explains how housing affordability has changed the Australian housing cycle. Young adults once typically left home, rented and saved, bought a home and paid off their mortgage before retirement. They now often stay at home and rent for longer, with more people carrying mortgages into retirement. Low rental vacancies and high turnover also make secure long-term rentals harder to find.

title: Loggerhead Turtle
text: The loggerhead turtle is one of the world's largest turtle species, and a species that’s nearly distinct in the United States. These remarkable creatures are easy to recognize thanks to their large, robust heads and relatively short necks, traits that set them apart from other sea turtle species. A key part of the loggerhead turtle’s life cycle is migration, which they undertake specifically to lay their eggs. To learn more about this migration, scientists conducted an important study back in September 1986. They attached a tracker to a loggerhead turtle’s shell and used satellite technology to closely monitor and locate its migration route—this was a groundbreaking way to map the turtle’s movements in real time. What did the study reveal? The turtle traveled to different locations at different times throughout its journey. It took just one month for the turtle to swim south, and the entire migration—from South Florida all the way north—spanned three months in total. To visualize this path, a map of the U.S. East Coast was created, and on it, both the turtle’s exact migration route and the year of the study (1986) are clearly marked. This research not only confirmed the loggerhead’s impressive migration abilities but also provided valuable data that helps protect these unique turtles and their habitats.
facts: Loggerhead turtles have large heads and relatively short necks.
Loggerheads migrate to lay eggs.
Researchers attached a tracker to a turtle’s shell in September 1986 and followed its route by satellite.
The lecture reports a month of southward travel and a total migration of three months.
Mapping the route provides data that can help protect the turtles and their habitats.
sample: The lecture describes the loggerhead turtle, recognizable by its large head and short neck, and its migration to lay eggs. In September 1986 researchers tracked a turtle by satellite and mapped its route on the U.S. East Coast. It swam south for a month during a three-month migration. This information can help protect loggerheads and their habitats.

title: Melatonin
text: I'm just going to take on where stuff left off. The hormone I want to now talk about it's called melatonin. The synthesis is in the Pineal Gland, which is very small. It is the size of a pea in your brain. Descartes called it the ‘seat of soul’, and it is where melatonin is made. And it has a rhythm as well. And in the sense, it is the opposite of the cortisol. It peaks at night. We call it as the darkness hormone. In every species that we studied, melatonin occurs at night. And it's hormone that prepares you for the things, that your species, does at night. So, of course, in humans we sleep, but animals, like rodents, they are awake. So, it's a hormone that is related to darkness behavior.
facts: Melatonin is made in the small pineal gland in the brain.
Its daily rhythm peaks at night, when the speaker calls it a darkness hormone.
Melatonin helps prepare a species for its typical nighttime behaviour.
The lecture contrasts sleeping humans with rodents that are active at night.
sample: The speaker explains that the pea-sized pineal gland produces melatonin. It follows a daily rhythm and peaks at night, leading to the name darkness hormone. It prepares each species for its usual behaviour after dark. The lecturer contrasts humans, who generally sleep at night, with rodents, which may be active then.

title: Invention
text: All of my research, and, that I conducted was my 60 plus graduate students, was motivated by their need to learn, so that we can teach. Of course, um, some inventions happened along the way but I've always considered the end, the result. And I always consider these inventions to be byproduct, byproducts of the learning process. The end product for me was always better understanding or when one really succeeded in unifying theory that can help us in teaching the subject. I've also looked at teaching as a vehicle to try new ideas, of new ways to doing things on an intelligent group of learners. That is as the vehicle for the teaching research results. And in my experience, this kind of teaching is the most stimulating and motivating to students. I've also uncovered many interesting research problems in the course of teaching assumption. It is this unity of research and teaching, their close connection, and the benefits garnered by exercising and the interplay that to me characterizes the successful professor.
facts: The speaker’s research with graduate students was motivated by learning and teaching.
Inventions emerged as by-products and a better understanding or unified theory was the main goal.
Teaching gives researchers a way to test new ideas with learners.
Teaching can motivate students and reveal fresh research problems.
sample: The speaker describes research and teaching as mutually supportive. Work with graduate students aimed to improve understanding and develop theories that could be taught. Inventions sometimes emerged along the way. Teaching also gave the professor a chance to test new ideas and discover further research problems. The lecturer sees that interplay as a feature of successful university teaching.

title: Springtime
text: The Earth's temperature is rising. And as it does, springtime phenomena—like the first bloom of flowers—are getting earlier and earlier. But rising temperatures aren't the only factor. Urban light pollution is also quickening the coming of spring. "So temperature and light are really contributing to a double whammy of making everything earlier.” Richard ffrench-Constant, an entomologist at the University of Exeter. He and his colleagues compiled 13 years of data from citizen scientists in the U.K., who tracked the first bud burst of four common trees. Turns out, light pollution—from streetlights in cities, and along roads—pushed bud burst a full week earlier. Way beyond what rising temperatures could achieve. This disruptive timing can ripple through the ecosystem. "The caterpillars that feed on trees are trying to match the hatching of their eggs to the timing of bud burst. Because the caterpillars want to feed on the juiciest and least chemically protected leaves. And it's not just the caterpillars, of course, that are important. But the knock-on effect is on nesting birds, which are also trying to hatch their chicks at the same time that there's the maximum number of caterpillars." So earlier buds could ultimately affect the survival of birds, and beyond. The findings are in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The world's becoming increasingly urbanized, and light pollution is growing—which ffrench-Constant says could trick trees into budding earlier and earlier. But smarter lighting—like LEDs that dial down certain wavelengths—could help. “Perhaps the exciting thing is, if we understand more about how light affects this bud burst, we might be able to devise smarter sort of street lighting that has less red components, and therefore less early bud burst." Thus keeping springtime an actual springtime phenomenon.
facts: Warming and artificial light both contribute to earlier spring events.
Researchers used 13 years of UK citizen observations of bud burst in four common trees.
Street lighting was associated with bud burst a week earlier.
Early budding can disrupt the timing of caterpillar hatching and food availability for nesting birds.
Street lighting with reduced red wavelengths may limit the effect.
sample: The lecture explains that warming and urban lighting are bringing spring events forward. Thirteen years of UK observations showed that artificial light advanced tree bud burst by about a week. That shift can disrupt caterpillars’ access to young leaves and the food supply of nesting birds. The researchers suggest street lighting with less red light could reduce this effect.

title: London Taxi Drivers
text: But we can really thank the Great Exhibition of 1851 for giving us the world’s premier taxi service, for it was going to this exhibition, and this fabulous exhibition inventions from all around the four corners of the Empire that the visitors were appalled, dismayed and vexed by their journeys to this exhibition because the cabbies of the day, and their horse-drawn carts were absolutely terrible, could not find their way to this exhibition. And, so, a great public outcry, the London Authority sets up Public Carriage Office, which is an organization that still exists. And you can take a short walk to Penton Street up the road. And this Public Carriage office took on the responsibility of licensing all major taxi drivers in London. All taxi drivers from 1851 onwards had to pass what is now known as the London knowledge, was phenomenal knowledge of London. What is the London knowledge? It’s the ability to remember the 25,000 streets, have it all interconnected and all the main arterial roads in and out of London. Cabbies need to know all this plus a thousand points of specific interest cafes, bars, public offices. They need to know them all as part of their training.
facts: The speaker traces changes in London taxi service to the Great Exhibition of 1851.
Poor journeys in horse-drawn cabs prompted public complaints and a move to licensing.
The Public Carriage Office took responsibility for licensing taxi drivers.
The Knowledge covers around 25,000 streets, connecting roads and about a thousand points of interest.
sample: The speaker traces London taxi licensing to complaints about cabs at the 1851 Great Exhibition. Drivers had trouble finding the venue, and the Public Carriage Office took on licensing. Drivers had to learn the Knowledge, which covers about 25,000 streets, their connections and main routes, plus around a thousand landmarks and other points of interest.

title: Music and Wellbeing
text: So what do we mean by well-being? Health, happiness, a sense of achievement and contentment, a state of mind and body where people can thrive. Well-being is not something that is purely limited to people who are facing extraordinary challenges in their lifestyle, health or personal circumstances, everybody here has a level of well-being. Music so often forms an intuitive part of our well-being management, music to pick us up, music to calm us down, music to heal our sorrows. Our aim through research is to move from this level of intuitive application of music through to informed use in our communities to take the next step in the understanding of the power of music in human life. Music already works for us on so many levels whether it's soothing and teaching our infants bringing people and communities together adding spirit to our work and personal endeavors, but there is no reason to stop here.
facts: Wellbeing includes health, happiness, achievement and the ability to thrive.
Everyone has a level of wellbeing and people often use music intuitively to manage it.
Music can lift or calm moods, soothe and teach infants, and bring communities together.
Research aims to help communities use music in more informed ways.
sample: The lecturer describes wellbeing as a state of physical and mental health, happiness and fulfilment. People already use music to lift their mood, calm down or cope with sadness. Music can also teach and soothe infants and bring people together. The speaker wants research to turn this intuitive use into informed practice for communities.

title: London Fog
text: Turner, not surprisingly, painted one of the earliest pictures of London's fog, in the 1835 painting the Thames above Waterloo Bridge. Turner is a trueborn Londoner, is advertising his familiarity with London's air problem by putting smoke, an atmospheric pollution at its center. And as you can see, in here, the bridge is the central element, which is a theme that's later taken up by Monet. And it's partly obscured by the steam and smoke which rises from both sides of the river. Here, we see a shot-tower. I think you can just about to see, which was constructed in 1826. Do you know what shot-towers are? They produce shot for guns, ammunition. And they were very smoky, one of the more smoky industries. But it's barely visible, as you can see, as are the various industries on the Lambuth side of the river. There's, on this side, there's a steamship about to dock or preparing to leave. It's black smoke thrusting up to join the kind of swirling arc of smoke there. William Rodner sees this painting as a potent essay on the energy and complexity of modern polluted organism. Smoke, I think, here represents for a flourishing economy, which brings employment and food on tables but also the dirt and pollution associated with the fumes all seems to be tainted by sulfurous yellow.
facts: Turner portrayed London’s fog in a painting of the Thames and Waterloo Bridge in 1835.
Smoke and steam partly obscure the bridge at the centre of the painting.
The lecture points to a shot tower, riverside industries and a steamship as elements of the scene.
The smoke evokes industrial activity and employment alongside dirt and atmospheric pollution.
sample: The lecturer discusses Turner’s 1835 painting of the Thames above Waterloo Bridge. Steam and smoke partly obscure the bridge, and the scene includes a shot tower, industry and a steamship. The lecturer interprets the smoke as a sign of a thriving economy that provides jobs, while the yellow haze shows the associated dirt and air pollution.

title: Night Sky Darkness
text: Our friends at the Highlands Museum and Discovery Center in Ashland, Kentucky, asked a very good question. Why is it dark in space? That question is not as simple as it may sound. You might think that space appears dark at night because that is when our side of Earth faces away from the Sun as our planet rotates on its axis every 24 hours. But what about all those other far away suns that appear as stars in the night sky? Our own Milky Way galaxy contains over 200 billion stars, and the entire universe probably contains over 100 billion galaxies. You might suppose that that many stars would light up the night like daytime! Until the 20th century, astronomers didn't think it was even possible to count all the stars in the universe. They thought the universe went on forever. In other words, they thought the universe was infinite. Besides being very hard to imagine, the trouble with an infinite universe is that no matter where you look in the night sky, you should see a star. Stars should overlap each other in the sky like tree trunks in the middle of a very thick forest. But, if this were the case, the sky would be blazing with light. This problem greatly troubled these astronomers and became known as “Olbers' Paradox." A paradox is a statement that seems to disagree with itself. To try to explain the paradox, some 19th century scientists thought that dust clouds between the stars must be absorbing a lot of the starlight so it wouldn't shine through to us. But later scientists realized that the dust itself would absorb so much energy from the starlight that eventually it would glow as hot and bright as the stars themselves. Astronomers now realize that the universe is not infinite. A finite universe—that is, a universe of limited size—even one with trillions and trillions of stars, just wouldn't have enough stars to light up all of space. Although the idea of a finite universe explains why Earth's sky is dark at night, other causes work to make it even darker.
facts: The lecture asks why space looks dark despite the enormous number of stars and galaxies.
An infinite universe filled with stars would appear bright in every direction, the puzzle called Olbers’ paradox.
Dust absorbing starlight would eventually become hot and glow, so dust alone cannot resolve the paradox.
The speaker’s explanation emphasizes that the universe has a limited number of stars and mentions other causes of darkness.
sample: The lecture explains why the night sky is dark despite the vast number of stars. In an infinite universe packed with stars, every line of sight should reach a star. This is Olbers’ paradox. Dust cannot solve it because heated dust would glow. The lecturer points instead to the limited number of stars and mentions other effects that deepen the darkness.

title: Marshmallow Test
text: Let's take a look at this video of these little kids. They were offered the option of having one marshmallow immediately or two marshmallows 15 minutes later and you've got some very cute video tape of this experiment. So let's take a look. What we found is a very simple and direct way of measuring a competence that seems to make an important life difference. A researcher tells these preschoolers that she's going to leave the room. If they wait for her to come back without eating the marshmallows, they'll get two marshmallows. Or, they can ring the bell and she'll come back right away but then they only get one marshmallow. I would ring the bell. You won't ring the bell? Okay. Looking at children over time, Dr. Michelle has found that being able to wait longer at four has some pretty powerful implications. And what are those powerful implications? Is that later in life they're more disciplined and have more self-control? Is that pretty much it. Well, they are more likely to achieve their life goals. They have better relationships. They do better on their SAT. Is that crazy all because they waited 15 minutes for two marshmallows? Well, I mean I think it is crazy. I probably would have eaten all three. Yeah, me too. But, um, you know, actually, yes, the ability to be able to pursue your goals, in this case, was that two marshmallows versus one, and not going automatic and just grab the marshmallow, is a very important skill. But I think a main point in mind in the making is that these skills can be caught, taught. If you're 14 or 40 or four it's not ever too late, and any child can learn, any adult can teach them. And it's never too late.
facts: Preschool children could take one marshmallow immediately or wait 15 minutes for two.
Ringing a bell brought the researcher back immediately and meant receiving one marshmallow.
The discussion links the ability to wait at age four with later self-control, relationships and achievement.
The speakers emphasize that pursuing goals and delaying a reward are skills people can learn.
sample: The speakers discuss an experiment in which preschoolers could take one marshmallow immediately or wait 15 minutes for two. Ringing a bell ended the wait with one marshmallow. They describe links between waiting and later achievement, relationships and self-control. The discussion ends by emphasizing that the ability to delay a reward and pursue a goal can be taught.

title: Bomb Calorimeter
text: This is a bomb calorimeter; this is the actual piece of equipment that researchers used to calculate the energy content of either biodiesel or maybe even the potato chips that you had for lunch today. When they calculate the amount of energy. They're going to calculate it in heat unites which would either be joules or calories. I want you to look inside the bomb calorimeter inside here, you can see that there's a silver bucket water goes all in here and this is actually the bomb is the smaller silver cylinder what you do is put your fuel sample in there then these two electrodes are connected to the bomb. These provide the spark that will ignite your sample when your sample burns or combust that gives off energy. So how is the energy collected or how did a scientist figure out how much energy is being given off. Well, it’s a closed system, there's a lid here that goes on top of this calorimeter and what's in here in the lid is a stirrer. The stir is going to stir the water. That's in this big pool here so that the heat given off from the sample is going to warm the water in a uniform way. This is the temperature probe, this goes down in the water also and measures the change in temperature because as the sample is burned, it will give off heat and the temperature the water will increase. So the lid goes on the sample is prepared. The last thing that you need to make a combustion reaction happen is oxygen and at some point during the process, some oxygen is added by a tank. That's connected to the calorimeter here. So we are going to burn a sample of the biodiesel that you've prepared and get some feedback on the energy content of it. You'll be able to use this to compare it to petroleum-based fuels like octane.
facts: A bomb calorimeter measures the energy content of samples such as foods or fuels.
Combustion in the sealed sample vessel releases heat into surrounding water.
Stirring distributes the heat and a probe measures the resulting rise in water temperature.
The measurement helps compare biodiesel with a petroleum fuel such as octane.
sample: The lecture explains how a bomb calorimeter measures the energy in a fuel or food sample. Burning the sample in a sealed vessel transfers heat to water around it. A stirrer spreads the heat evenly and a probe measures the rise in temperature. The speaker gives comparing biodiesel and octane as an application of the method.

title: Infinite Monkey Theorem
text: This illustration often used is the one that the monkeys and the typewriters. Ok, we have a monkey sitting at a typewriter and the claim here is basically if you leave chance in time long enough you will get life. Don't worry about it. Yes, its's strange. Yes, it's wonderful. But leave enough matter 600 million years on earth and you will have life. So, the monkey sitting at the typewriter, the chances are eventually he produces the complete works of Shakespeare. So what's the problem. But he doesn't manage to do it in 600 million years. So, what I decided to do is run the numbers. I, instead of saying typing the complete work of Shakespeare, I just run the numbers for how long would it take a monkey, typing one key striker a second, to type ‘to be or not to be that is the question’. Right? On average how long is it gonna take my monkey friend one keystroke a second. I don't know how you think it would be. Maybe you could have a guess. Would it be less or more than 600 million years, which is the period life on earth isn't supposed to have emerged within. And when I run the numbers ‘to be or not to be is the question’ takes 12.6 trillion trillion trillion years to type just that phrase. And a DNA string, that complexity, emerges by chance undirected within 600 million years. Again, it's mathematically possible but it's so incredibly unlikely that, it would have, that it tilts me in favor of the Christian story in which God creating life, simply a question of saying let that be and there was.
facts: The lecture uses the analogy of a monkey randomly typing Shakespeare to discuss chance over long periods.
The speaker considers one keystroke per second and a short quotation from Shakespeare.
The speaker estimates 12.6 trillion trillion trillion years for the phrase and contrasts it with 600 million years.
The speaker uses the comparison to question an undirected origin of life and favour a Christian account.
sample: The lecturer uses the monkey and typewriter analogy to discuss chance. At one keystroke per second, the speaker calculates that typing a short Shakespeare quotation would take an extraordinarily long time, far longer than 600 million years. The speaker uses that comparison to question whether life arose through undirected chance and expresses a preference for a Christian explanation.

title: Trade-off Triangle
text: Well, it's about whether you can achieve a win-win solution, whether you can achieve economic growth which brings wealth in order to cut poverty without damaging the biodiversity. And the argument is that if you want to protect biodiversity, you have to focus on that as a goal; but if you do that, you have ... you run the risk of hurting the poor and you also run the risk of inconveniencing and reducing the economic growth. We use the developed and industrialized countries to see this argument, this axis argued about with, let us say, a government wishing to start drilling for oil in place X which is full of wildlife, and wildlife conservation society is urging them not to on the grounds that it's a wilderness refuge. We use to that debate. What I'm saying is that in the developing world there's a third axis and it's a complex one.
facts: The lecture asks whether growth can reduce poverty while protecting biodiversity.
Focusing on conservation can affect economic growth and the livelihoods of poor people.
Oil drilling in a wildlife refuge illustrates the growth and conservation conflict in developed economies.
In the developing world, poverty adds a distinct dimension to the policy choice.
sample: The lecturer asks whether economic growth can reduce poverty while protecting biodiversity. A conservation decision may limit economic activity and hurt poor communities. The speaker uses proposed oil drilling in a wildlife refuge as an example of the familiar growth and conservation debate. In developing countries, poverty adds a third consideration and makes the trade-off more complex.
